summary.text: Special relativity is a theory built on two postulates: physics works the same in every non-accelerating frame, and light has the same speed for every observer.
It replaces the idea of one universal time with a time local to each observer, and it makes the speed of light the maximum possible speed.
Combined with other laws of physics, its two postulates predict that mass and energy are equivalent, as written in the formula E = mc².

facts.label: Two postulates
facts.value: Relativity principle and constant speed of light

facts.label: Galileo's ship
facts.value: Described the principle of relativity in 1632

facts.label: Famous prediction
facts.value: Mass and energy are equivalent: E = mc²

items.prompt: You stand on a station platform and measure the speed of light from a lamp on the platform, then from the headlight of a train rushing past. What do you find?

options.label: The train's light is faster by the train's own speed
The train's light is slower if the train moves away
Both beams are measured at the same speed
The platform lamp is faster since it is at rest

items.explain: The second postulate says light travels at the same speed for observers whatever the motion of the source.

items.prompt: A spaceship keeps firing its engines and doubles its speed again and again. Why can't it ever pass the speed that light has?

options.label: Its engines eventually run out of fuel to burn
The theory makes light's speed the top possible speed
Speeds stop adding up once an object is heavy
Space gets denser and slows fast ships down

items.explain: Special relativity builds light's speed in as the maximum, so speeds do not simply add the way everyday intuition says.

items.prompt: A friend films a very fast object flying past and says the footage shows exactly how its shape is changed by relativity. Why should you be cautious?

options.label: Cameras cannot record anything moving that fast
Relativity only affects what happens inside atoms
Light from far-off parts arrives later, so images show the past
Fast objects become invisible once they pass the viewer

items.explain: Information cannot arrive faster than light, so what is seen reports earlier events, which makes visual descriptions error-prone.

items.prompt: Two crews in fast ships each carry a clock. Before relativity, people assumed one shared time ticking for everyone. What does special relativity put in its place?

options.label: A time that belongs to each observer separately
A time set only by the slowest clock around
A time that is the average of all clocks
A time that stops for any moving observer

items.explain: The absolute, universal time is replaced by time that is local to each observer.

items.prompt: Physicists need to compare the coordinates of an event as seen from a rocket moving close to light speed with those seen from Earth. Which rule do they use?

options.label: The Galilean rule from Newton's mechanics
A simple adding of the two speeds together
The Pythagorean theorem on space only
The Lorentz rule that replaces the Galilean one

items.explain: For frames in relative motion, the Lorentz transformation replaces the Galilean transformation of Newtonian mechanics.

items.prompt: Two observers moving relative to each other each work out the spacetime interval between the same two events. What do they find?

options.label: The same value, whatever their relative velocity
Values that differ by their relative speed
Zero for whichever observer is moving
Values that differ only in their time part

items.explain: Unlike spatial distances, the interval between two events is the same for all observers.
